text:
Does the Risk Outweigh the Benefit?

WASHINGTON — Beyond the political fight over the DoD’s new testosterone screening mandate remains a clinical question: Does population-level screening of a mostly asymptomatic, young military population offer significant benefit or simply raise risk?

The memorandum directing the policy makes testosterone screening a mandatory element of the Periodic Health Assessment for active-duty and reserve personnel 30 and older, with screening optional for younger service members.

The memo’s clinical rationale leans heavily on “operator syndrome,” which refers to a constellation of issues tied in a 2020 study to the extreme physical and psychological demands characteristic of special operations careers, including chronic combat stress, repeated blast wave exposures, traumatic brain injuries, and chronic sleep deprivation.1

While often associated with a sharp drop in testosterone, operator syndrome is a complex pattern of health concerns including traumatic brain injury (TBI), sleep issues, obstructive sleep apnea, orthopedic problems, vestibular and vision impairments, headaches, and sexual health issues. It also captures a pattern of mental and social health concerns such as cognitive impairment, memory and concentration difficulties, substance abuse, depression, suicide, anger, anxiety, hyper vigilance, stress reactivity, and difficulty with the transition to civilian life as well as marital, family, and community dysfunction.

Given the range of symptoms and number of body systems affected, a holistic approach to affected individuals is recommended, starting with good nutrition, adequate sleep, treatment of diabetes and obesity, and stress management techniques. The original study on operator syndrome called for integrated neurological, medical, sleep, pain, psychiatric, genetic, microbiota, and metabolic assessment and treatment, and viewed low testosterone as a consequence of the rigors of SOF training and careers, not a cause of the syndrome itself.

There also remains a question of efficacy. A study of 50 men that tested supplemental testosterone (200 mg/wk) in short-term energy deficit conditions found that the therapy increased lean body mass but did not reduce lower-body muscle performance decline or improve health-related biomarkers.2 In addition, a small study of special operations forces (SOF) members who had experienced mild to moderate TBI concluded that “these findings indicate testosterone use may not significantly affect symptoms of chronic pain, chronic headache, insomnia, PTSD, anxiety, and depression.” The only difference found between those treated with testosterone and those who were not was a higher pain score in individuals receiving hormone therapy.3

An Ongoing Debate

The debate over testosterone predates the operator syndrome discussion by decades, however, and has focused primarily on safety.

Charles Huggins, MD, made his Nobel Prize-winning discovery that androgen deprivation shrank prostate cancer tumors in 1941.4 His seminal work included a conclusion based on one patient, that the converse was also true—testosterone supplementation stimulates prostate cancer.

A meta-analysis of studies from 1941 to 2008 found that the connection between exogenous testosterone and prostate cancer was far from linear, and that above the near-castrate range, there was little connection.5 (Another analysis in 2024 extended the findings, concluding that there was insufficient evidence of risk for increasing the aggressiveness of prostate cancer in men managed with active surveillance.)6

“Low-T” clinics rapidly multiplied, but new concerns emerged. Researchers prematurely discontinued a 2010 study in 209 older men because of elevated risk in a six-month period: 23 subjects in the testosterone group vs. five in the placebo group experienced cardiovascular-related adverse events. In 2013, a landmark VA study published in JAMA that enrolled 8,709 veterans, showed that hypogonadal men undergoing testosterone therapy had a 29% greater risk of death, heart attack, or stroke than those not on the hormone over an average follow-up period of 27.5 months.7 In both studies, the participants had a high rate of cardiovascular disease at initiation.

The FDA required testosterone products to carry warnings of cardiovascular risk in 2015.

In 2023, the industry-sponsored TRAVERSE trial in 5,246 men with hypogonadism and at risk for or with existing CVD challenged the findings from a decade earlier, showing no increase in cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or coronary revascularization with 33 months of follow up.8 A companion analysis of the same trial found roughly a 50% relative increase in pulmonary embolism and a higher fracture incidence among men on testosterone.

What the Guidelines Say

With that mixed background and the DoD mandate in mind, The Endocrine Society restated its clinical practice guidelines in July. Notably, the society maintained a conservative posture, saying, “there is insufficient evidence to support a general recommendation to perform population-level screening for hypogonadism in asymptomatic men with measurement of blood testosterone level.”

Diagnosing hypogonadism requires both symptoms of low testosterone and consistently low levels on accurately measured blood tests. Symptoms alone, the society notes, are also not diagnostic, as low energy, libido and mood have many causes in aging men, and reversible contributors such as obesity, corticosteroids, obstructive sleep apnea or opioid use need to be ruled out first.9

Testing accuracy compounds the diagnostic problem, the Society adds. Not all testosterone assays are standardized, so the same blood sample can read as low or normal depending on the lab and method used. The CDC’s Hormone Standardization (HoST) program was created to close this gap by certifying qualifying assays as harmonized.

Jason Goldman, MD, internal medicine physician and immediate past president of the American College of Physicians, put the frequent discordance between initial testing and diagnosis in concrete terms: up to 40% of men tested in one study had low readings, but fewer than 2% had any accompanying symptoms.10

Weighing Benefit Against Risk

The Endocrine Society considers the long-term prostate cancer risk unresolved, as it argues that trials have not followed patients long enough to detect it.11

Goldman said the new policy increases known risks. “Testosterone therapy can increase heart attack risk, thicken the blood, cause blood clots, worsen sleep apnea, cause weight gain, cause infertility, make people more aggressive, [and] can make prostate cancer worse,” Goldman said. “Just giving testosterone is not going to optimize troops but could cause severe harm. This is not good, sound medical strategy.”

Jeremy Samuel Faust, MD, emergency physician, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, assistant professor, Harvard Medical School, and editor-in-chief of MedPage raised another safety concern, with specific importance to a military population. “In the big trials, people at higher risk of suicide were excluded from the testosterone trials because of that fear,” Faust said. “I worry about that, and I think it’s really important that we keep our people safe.”12 He added that men with low testosterone but no symptoms “do not benefit from supplementation,” further weakening the case for screening asymptomatic servicemembers.

Beyond Debate

While the effect of testosterone therapy on CVD and cancer may remain unresolved, its impact on fertility is uncontroversial. Testosterone suppresses luteinizing hormone/follicle-stimulating hormone, which is absolutely critical for sperm development. Two World Health Organization studies found that testosterone supplementation for six months resulted in no measurable sperm in 65% to 98% of men.13 After discontinuation of testosterone therapy, about 65% of men recover to 20 million sperm/mL at six months and 100% at two years, though duration of treatment and age may make recovery more difficult.14 For young men at peak family formation age, impaired fertility represents a significant downside.

A separate strand of research complicates the picture further. A meta-analysis of 12 studies including more than 102,000 men presented July 7 at the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology found that total and free testosterone, along with sex hormone-binding globulin, have dropped significantly worldwide since 1972, with the rate of decline nearly doubling after 2000.15 Total testosterone plummeted 54%. Shifting population ranges raise questions about what counts as a normal testosterone level and treatment becomes more complex when “rising rates of obesity and metabolic disorders, exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals like phthalates or microplastics, sedentary lifestyles, unhealthy dietary patterns, and chronic psychosocial stress have all been implicated”16 in the decline.

None of this forecloses testosterone therapy for troops who are appropriately diagnosed. The Endocrine Society and the trial data agree that men with confirmed hypogonadism from a disease of the testes, pituitary or hypothalamus benefit from treatment at appropriate physiologic doses. The clinical debate now centers on whether mandating screening across a young, mostly asymptomatic population, using assays that are often not standardized, and without a clear protocol for what happens after a low reading, does more long-term harm than good.

Trying to understand insurance coverage for addiction treatment can feel overwhelming, especially when help is needed quickly — and TRICARE’s rules work differently than a typical commercial health plan. If you or someone you love is a service member, veteran, or military family member with TRICARE, learning how TRICARE drug rehab coverage works can help you take the next step with more confidence. This page explains what TRICARE plans may cover, how coverage decisions are made, and how Rebuilt Treatment & Recovery can help you navigate your benefits.

Substance use continues to affect military and veteran communities at meaningful rates. A 2022 Department of Defense report found that roughly 29 percent of active-duty service members engage in binge drinking, and substance use disorders remain significantly underdiagnosed and undertreated across the military health system. Insurance coverage plays a critical role in closing this treatment gap by making professional care more accessible.

TRICARE isn’t one single plan — coverage rules can vary depending on which of the following you or your family member is enrolled in:

TRICARE Prime — a managed-care option that typically requires a referral from your Primary Care Manager (PCM) and prior authorization before starting treatment

TRICARE Select — a preferred-provider option with more flexibility to see providers directly, though prior authorization may still apply for certain levels of care

TRICARE Reserve Select & TRICARE Retired Reserve — coverage options for qualifying National Guard and Reserve members and their families

TRICARE For Life — for Medicare-eligible retirees and their family members

TRICARE Young Adult — extends coverage to qualifying adult children of TRICARE sponsors

Washington State falls under the TRICARE West Region, administered by TriWest Healthcare Alliance as of January 2025. Confirming your specific plan and region helps us verify exactly what your benefits cover before you begin treatment.

Despite how common substance use disorders are, treatment access remains limited nationally — and military and veteran communities face additional, unique barriers, including stigma around seeking care and concerns about how treatment may affect a career or security clearance. National data shows that nearly 80 percent of people who need substance use treatment do not receive it, often due to financial concerns, insurance confusion, or difficulty navigating coverage.

Understanding your TRICARE drug rehab benefits — and working with a team experienced in military-specific coverage rules — can help reduce these barriers and make treatment more attainable.

TRICARE often supports evidence-based addiction treatment delivered in outpatient and partial hospitalization settings when services are deemed medically necessary and delivered by a TRICARE-authorized provider.

Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP)

Partial Hospitalization offers a highly structured level of day treatment — often several hours a day, most days of the week — for individuals who need more intensive support than outpatient care but don’t require 24-hour residential supervision. TRICARE commonly covers PHP when it’s clinically recommended.

Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP)

An Intensive Outpatient Program provides structured therapy several days per week while allowing individuals to live at home or in supportive housing. IOP is commonly covered by TRICARE and is often recommended for individuals who need consistent support without residential care, including many service members balancing treatment with duty station responsibilities.

Outpatient Program (OP)

Standard outpatient treatment typically involves fewer weekly therapy sessions focused on counseling and recovery skills. This level of care is often covered for individuals with a stable living environment who need ongoing clinical support.

These options allow individuals to continue working, training, attending school, or caring for family while receiving treatment.

TRICARE evaluates several factors when determining coverage for addiction treatment, including:

Medical necessity based on a clinical assessment

Diagnosis of a substance use disorder

Recommended level of care

Whether treatment is delivered by a TRICARE-authorized provider

Referral from your Primary Care Manager, if required by your plan

Any required prior authorization

It’s also worth knowing that TRICARE places specific limits on certain substance use disorder rehabilitation benefits, including caps on the number of covered treatment episodes over a beneficiary’s lifetime. These limits vary by the type of care and setting, which is exactly why insurance verification matters — it clarifies what’s covered, for how long, and what, if anything, has already been used toward any lifetime limits.

BETHESDA, MD — While it is understood that problematic alcohol use (PAU) and anxiety disorders (ANX) often co-occur, suggesting some type of shared genetic and neurobiological foundations, the directionality of potential causal relationships and the specific mechanisms have remained unclear.

That led to the investigation of the shared genetic architecture and neurobiological pathways between PAU and ANX using a multimethod genomic approach. The research was led by the Uniformed Services University in Bethesda, MD. Other federal medicine investigators were from the Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine Inc. in Bethesda, MD,the Crescenz VAMC in Philadelphia and the VA Connecticut Healthcare System in West Haven, CT.

The study team analyzed summary statistics from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of PAU and ANX using Mendelian Randomization to assess causal associations between ANX and PAU. MiXeR was employed to assess the overall shared genomic architecture, Local Analysis of (co)Variant Association to estimate regional genetic correlations, and conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR) to identify individual overlapping loci. The researchers said they also Functional Mapping and Annotation (FUMA) to map single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to independent loci, conduct differential gene expression analyses across 30 general and 54 specific tissue types and perform cell-type specificity analyses using a human brain cell atlas. Druggability of identified targets also 1was evaluated, they said.

In results published in the journal Neuropsychopharmacology, Mendelian Randomization analyses indicated bidirectional causal associations between ANX and PAU. In addition, MiXeR identified moderate polygenic overlap (52.5%) and genetic correlation (rg = 0.44) between the traits, with high effect direction concordance among shared estimated causal variants (86.4%). The study team explained that ConjFDR identified 97 shared lead SNPs, of which 89 had concordant and 8 discordant effects on PAU and ANX.

“These loci mapped to 97 genes, including DRD2 and PDE4B, genes linked to dopaminergic and cAMP signaling pathways, respectively,” according to the authors. “Concordant gene expression was enriched in brain, nerve, adrenal gland, esophagus, stomach, and colon, with enriched expression specifically in the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, substantia nigra and amygdala. FUMA cell-type enrichment analysis identified associations predominantly in neurons from the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus.”

The researchers concluded, “We found substantial genetic and neurobiological overlap between PAU and ANX, highlighting reciprocal, causal relationships between the traits, with differentially expressed genes enriched in addiction- and anxiety-relevant brain regions. These findings support shared genetic and neurobiological mechanisms linking PAU and ANX, while acknowledging that some signals may reflect broader internalizing or psychiatric liability.”

title: Million Veterans Database Used in Large-Scale Analysis for Cardiometabolic Traits
description:
Los Angeles — Noting that studies linking mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) with complex traits are often limited by small sample sizes or focused on specific phenotypes in clinically selected cohorts, researchers recently reported data from more than 600,000 participants in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) to perform a multiancestry analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variation and cardiometabolic phenotypes across European (EUR), African (AFR), Admixed American (AMR) and East Asian (EAS) populations.
The study team, which was led by UCLA Fielding School of Public Health, validated 248 mtDNA loci and then identified 10 ancestry-stratified single-variant associations (8 EUR, 2 AFR) and 23 additional signals in sex- and Type 2 diabetes (T2D)-stratified analyses.
Co-authors included VA researchers from Phoenix; Boston; Philadelphia; Salt Lake City; Providence, RI; Nashville, TN; Atlanta; and Palo Alto, CA.
“Gene-based rare-variant tests (minor allele frequency ≤2%) yield 26 associations (12 EUR, 10 AFR, 2 AMR, 2 EAS), including mitochondrial tRNA burdens linked to primary cardiomyopathy (females) and exophthalmos (males).
Twenty-three of the 33 single-variant signals map to the endocrine/metabolic category, indicating significant enrichment (Fisher’s exact P = 0.003).” The authors concluded, “These results define ancestry- and context-specific contributions of mtDNA to cardiometabolic disease, with a notable concentration in endocrine traits, and provide a framework for mtDNA analysis across diverse biobank cohorts.”

Los Angeles — Noting that studies linking mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) with complex traits are often limited by small sample sizes or focused on specific phenotypes in clinically selected cohorts, researchers recently reported data from more than 600,000 participants in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) to perform a multiancestry analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variation and cardiometabolic phenotypes across European (EUR), African (AFR), Admixed American (AMR) and East Asian (EAS) populations.

The study team, which was led by UCLA Fielding School of Public Health, validated 248 mtDNA loci and then identified 10 ancestry-stratified single-variant associations (8 EUR, 2 AFR) and 23 additional signals in sex- and Type 2 diabetes (T2D)-stratified analyses. Co-authors included VA researchers from Phoenix; Boston; Philadelphia; Salt Lake City; Providence, RI; Nashville, TN; Atlanta; and Palo Alto, CA.

The results published in Nature Communications indicated that four variants tagging haplogroup J, D-loop MT228G > A, MT-ND3 MT10398A > G (p.Thr114Ala), MT-ND5 MT13708G > A (p.Ala458Thr), and MT-CYB MT14798T > C (p.Phe18Leu), are associated with hypothyroidism in EUR and replicated in UK Biobank (UKBB) with concordant effects.1

“In EUR females, MT-RNR1 MT1555A > G increases the risk of carditis and heart failure phenotypes, supporting prior reports of maternally inherited cardiomyopathy,” the study explains. “Gene-based rare-variant tests (minor allele frequency ≤2%) yield 26 associations (12 EUR, 10 AFR, 2 AMR, 2 EAS), including mitochondrial tRNA burdens linked to primary cardiomyopathy (females) and exophthalmos (males). Twenty-three of the 33 single-variant signals map to the endocrine/metabolic category, indicating significant enrichment (Fisher’s exact P = 0.003).”

The authors concluded, “These results define ancestry- and context-specific contributions of mtDNA to cardiometabolic disease, with a notable concentration in endocrine traits, and provide a framework for mtDNA analysis across diverse biobank cohorts.”

text:
Georgia Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock have sent a new letter to War Department officials demanding they immediately withdraw a formal notification to Congress about modifying services at Eisenhower Army Medical Center, arguing that servicemembers, their families and veterans around Augusta deserve answers before any changes move forward. The senators say the Defense Health Agency plans to convert the hospital into an ambulatory care center, a shift that would permanently shut down inpatient care and downgrade the emergency room to an urgent care facility.

According to Atlanta News First, the senators wrote that 17 days had passed since a response deadline they set in June without any reply from the War Department, calling the silence unacceptable. The August 7 letter, addressed to Assistant Secretary of Defense Keith Bass and Defense Health Agency Director Vice Adm. Darin Via, followed the agency's failure to respond within the deadline to a prior inquiry, according to Senator Jon Ossoff's office. Ossoff had also raised concerns about the proposed reductions in a separate letter sent to the agency in November 2025.

What's at Stake for Augusta-Area Patients

Eisenhower Army Medical Center, also known as Dwight D. Eisenhower Army Medical Center, sits near Augusta and provides care to an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 beneficiaries across the Central Savannah River Area, per Senator Ossoff's office. Local healthcare leaders and lawmakers have warned that eliminating inpatient and emergency services would redirect patients to already-strained civilian providers, including Wellstar MCG Health and the Charlie Norwood VA Medical Center, according to the same account from Senator Raphael Warnock's office.

The hospital operates roughly 60 inpatient beds and six operating rooms, with a staff of about 1,500 people, including approximately 80 medical residents who make up roughly half of its physician workforce, per Ossoff's office. Those residents train across five graduate medical education programs — Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Orthopedic Surgery, General Surgery and Transitional Year. Ossoff and Warnock say the proposed changes could disrupt medical care for servicemembers, their families and veterans while adding strain to Augusta's civilian health care system.

A Legal Fight Over Notification Timing

Under 10 U.S.C. §1073d, the Department of Defense must submit a detailed report to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees before modifying or downsizing a military medical treatment facility, triggering a mandatory 180-day congressional review period before changes can take effect, according to the Congressional Research Service. In May, a bipartisan group of six U.S. Representatives — led by Rep. Rick Allen and Rep. Joe Wilson alongside Reps. Austin Scott, Buddy Carter, Brian Jack and Sheri Biggs — sent a joint letter to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth accusing the Defense Health Agency of circumventing the law by starting downsizing before completing statutory review requirements, per the Office of Representative Rick Allen. Allen, a Republican representing Augusta, and his office said the lawmakers emphasized that more than 20 military installations sit within the region their letter represented.

Ossoff and Warnock argue the Pentagon has not fully explained which services would be affected or how the transition would actually work. The House Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel responded to that uncertainty by inserting language into the draft Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act in June to halt service reductions and closures at 41 military treatment facilities nationwide, including Eisenhower, while requiring quarterly status reports from the Defense Health Agency, according to the Military Officers Association of America. Allen's office said the provisions were aimed in part at protecting Eisenhower Army Medical Center, and he has backed those provisions in the House-passed defense bill.

Part of a Bigger Pentagon Overhaul

The push to restructure Eisenhower traces back to a Department of Defense plan released in February 2020 under Section 703 of the FY2017 NDAA, which designated 50 military hospitals and clinics nationwide for downsizing to prioritize active-duty combat readiness over retiree and dependent care, according to the Air Force Medical Service. Out of 343 domestic military medical facilities screened that year, 50 were selected for realignment. A Government Accountability Office study, first published in 2020 and updated in June 2023, found the Defense Health Agency lacked adequate data to ensure civilian medical networks could absorb transferred military beneficiaries and had no established mechanism to reverse downsizing if local civilian care proved insufficient.

Fort Eisenhower, renamed from Fort Gordon in 2023, hosts the U.S. Army Cyber Center of Excellence, U.S. Army Cyber Command and NSA Georgia, supporting an installation population of more than 16,000 active-duty military members and 13,500 civilian personnel, according to Wikipedia. Notably, the Department of War itself named Eisenhower Army Medical Center one of 15 military hospitals nationwide to receive an A hospital safety grade from The Leapfrog Group for its spring 2026 evaluation, even as the same department pursues plans to strip the hospital of its inpatient operations.

text:
What TRICARE Actually Covers for Dialysis Rides

TRICARE covers dialysis transportation only when it's medically necessary ambulance service, not routine wheelchair-van or ambulette trips. For Long Island beneficiaries — active-duty families, retirees, and their dependents — TRICARE will generally pay for an ambulance if your condition requires clinical monitoring en route, such as an unstable transfer after a hospital stay. But the everyday, three-times-a-week trip to a chair at a dialysis center in Nassau or Suffolk is considered "non-emergency medical transportation" (NEMT), which TRICARE typically does not reimburse. That distinction matters because dialysis is a recurring, scheduled treatment, not an emergency. Understanding the line between an ambulance and an ambulette helps you avoid a surprise bill; our guide on ambulette vs. ambulance vs. wheelchair van breaks down exactly which vehicle fits your medical need. If you're mobile but need a safe, reliable seat, standard dialysis transportation through DachiPlus is usually the right fit — and far more affordable than an ambulance. Always confirm your specific plan (TRICARE Prime, Select, or For Life) before assuming coverage.

TRICARE vs. VA Community Care for Veterans on Long Island

Many Long Island veterans have better luck getting dialysis rides through VA Community Care than through TRICARE. TRICARE is health insurance for the military community, while VA Community Care is a program that arranges — and often pays for — care and transportation for veterans enrolled with the VA. If you receive dialysis at a community center in towns like Bay Shore, Commack, or Deer Park, VA Community Care may authorize recurring transport when VA facilities can't provide it directly. DachiPlus works with veterans under VA Community Care coverage, and our veterans medical transportation service is built for exactly this kind of scheduled treatment. Veterans who also qualify for Medicaid may layer benefits. For a full rundown of options — from VA-arranged rides to community providers — see transportation options for VA health appointments and our overview of veteran support. If you served and now need dialysis three times a week in Suffolk County, don't assume TRICARE is your only door — VA Community Care is frequently the more practical path.

If TRICARE Won't Cover It: Medicaid and MAS on Long Island

When TRICARE doesn't cover your routine dialysis rides, New York Medicaid — coordinated through MAS — is the most common backup for eligible Long Island patients. If you have NY Medicaid (or a dual-eligible plan alongside TRICARE), transportation to and from dialysis is a covered benefit statewide. You book it by calling MAS, the state's transportation broker, at 1-844-666-6270 — the NYS Medicaid transportation phone number — at least 72 hours before your appointment and requesting DachiPlus by name. Because dialysis is recurring, MAS can set up a standing order so you don't have to call before every trip. Our MAS Medicaid guide and the step-by-step Medicaid coverage walkthrough explain enrollment, the 72-hour rule, and standing orders in plain language. Eligibility isn't based on the federal poverty level alone — New York has its own income and category rules — so if you're unsure, review who qualifies for Medicaid transportation. Patients across Nassau and Suffolk rely on this route for treatment at Fresenius and DaVita centers every week.

Private Pay, Medicare Advantage, and No-Fault Alternatives

If neither TRICARE nor Medicaid applies, private pay, Medicare Advantage, or no-fault auto coverage can still get you to dialysis reliably. Private pay coverage lets you book directly with DachiPlus using a credit or debit card, HSA, or FSA — call (516) 754-7777 to set up a recurring weekly schedule. If your dialysis need followed a car crash, no-fault auto coverage and our no-fault accident transportation may pay for the trips. Retirees with Medicare should note that Original Medicare and Medicare Part D (which covers prescription drugs, not routine rides) rarely help — but many Medicare Advantage plans bundle a transportation benefit. Our comparison of Medicaid vs. private pay helps you weigh cost and convenience. Long-term care policyholders can also check long-term care insurance coverage. Whatever your funding source, DachiPlus provides wheelchair-accessible transport with transfer-to-seat assistance and secured wheelchairs — a safer, more predictable option than wheelchair taxis or standard rideshare for kidney patients across Long Island.

Booking Recurring Dialysis Transport Across Nassau & Suffolk

Recurring dialysis transport works best when you set a standing schedule with a provider that already serves your center's town. DachiPlus operates Monday through Saturday, 6 AM to 8 PM, covering hamlets and villages throughout Nassau County and Suffolk County — from Bay Shore and Commack to Selden and Smithtown. Does TRICARE cover dialysis transportation on Long Island?

TRICARE generally covers medically necessary ambulance transport, but routine, non-emergency dialysis rides (ambulette or wheelchair van) are typically not a standard TRICARE benefit. What's the difference between TRICARE and VA Community Care for dialysis rides?

TRICARE is health coverage for active-duty and retired service members and families, while VA Community Care arranges care and transportation for enrolled veterans through the VA. Many Long Island veterans get dialysis rides authorized through VA Community Care rather than TRICARE.

Who do I call to book non-emergency dialysis transportation?

For private pay, workers' comp, no-fault, VA Community Care, or Medicare Advantage, call DachiPlus at (516) 754-7777. If you have NY Medicaid, call MAS at 1-844-666-6270 — the NYS Medicaid transportation phone number — at least 72 hours ahead and request DachiPlus.

Does TRICARE for Life help with dialysis transport if I also have Medicare?

If you have Medicare plus TRICARE for Life, Medicare is primary. Original Medicare rarely covers routine ambulette dialysis rides, but a Medicare Advantage plan may include a transportation benefit. Confirm your specific plan before booking.

Can DachiPlus take me to a specific dialysis center in Suffolk County?

Yes. DachiPlus provides recurring wheelchair-accessible and ambulette-style transport to centers across Nassau and Suffolk — including Fresenius Bay Shore, Fresenius Commack, DaVita Smithtown, and DaVita Selden — on a set weekly schedule.

text:
ST. LOUIS — Even though tumor comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) has revolutionized the care of many cancers and identifies patients for biomarker-specific therapy, it had not been available for all variations.

For example, in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC), “although individual genes are prognostic, no comprehensive genomic classification exists using CGP that accounts for combinations of alterations to inform prognosis,” according to a new study in JCO Precision Oncology.1

In response, a study team led by Saint Louis University School of Medicine and the VA St Louis Healthcare System developed a DNA-based CGP classification that is prognostic for overall survival (OS) and could inform treatment. Other VA researchers contributing were from James A. Haley Veterans’ Hospital in Tampa, FL; the Puget Sound VA Healthcare System in Seattle; the Corporal Michael Crescenz VAMC in Philadelphia; the VA Salt Lake City, UT, Healthcare System; the VA Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System; the VA Boston Healthcare System; the VA San Diego Healthcare System; the Durham, NC, VAMC‘ and the VA National Oncology Program in Washington, DC.

The retrospective cross-sectional study used multivariable models to develop a clinicogenomic prognostic risk classification in U.S. veterans with synchronous mHSPC. Defined as the primary outcome was overall survival from time of metastasis.

Identified were 7,201 veterans with metastatic prostate cancer and CGP; 2,484 of the veterans—median age of 72 with synchronous mHSPC and tissue CGP—were divided into training and testing data sets. The researchers pinpointed 16 genes associated with survival and then created favorable, intermediate and unfavorable genomic prognostication groups based on the mortality risk to generate the Somatic Tumor Risk Assessment for OS-Prostate (STRATOS-P) classification.

“In a multivariable model, classification into intermediate and unfavorable groups was associated with increased mortality relative to the favorable group (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.54 [95% CI, 1.33 to 1.78]; aHR, 2.37 [95% CI, 1.97 to 2.485], respectively), demonstrating an average AUC of 0.83,” the study noted.

The authors advised, “In an external, nonveterans validation cohort, intermediate and unfavorable classifications were associated with increased mortality (aHR, 2.45 [95% CI, 1.87 to 3.21]; aHR, 4.37 [95% CI, 3.06 to 6.22], respectively) with an AUC of 0.79. The intermediate and unfavorable genomic prognostication groups were also associated with increased mortality across multiple disease states including synchronous and metachronous diagnoses, castration resistance, and analyte type.”

The study concluded that, in metastatic prostate cancer, tumor DNA genomic alterations are prognostic for overall survival. “The STRATOS-P classification is a validated prognostic tool that has the potential to guide decision making in mHSPC,” according to the researchers.

Background information in the article pointed out that tumor DNA alterations are fundamental to understanding cancer biology. Genomic testing can “inform clinical management, including the use of chemotherapy in early breast cancer. Similar integrative approaches in prostate cancer using RNA expression combined with clinical nomograms can improve prognostication and are being tested as potential predictive biomarkers,” they added.

text:
New Study Looks at Differing Practice Patterns by Gender

LOS ANGELES — Female and male physicians have different practice patterns, according to past studies mainly focused on primary care. One difference cited has been that women physicians are more likely to order diagnostic testing and provide more guideline-concordant care for conditions such as diabetes, as well as more preventive care.

It has not been clear, however, whether practice patterns differ in settings where selection between patients and physicians is more limited, such as emergency departments (EDs).

A new study published in JAMA Internal Medicine pointed out that smaller ED studies have found no differences in testing or hospital admission. To gain more information, a study team led by the VA Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System and the David Geffen School of Medicine at University of California, Los Angeles, recently used VA data to examine differences in test ordering and hospital admission between female and male physicians working in the same EDs.

The researchers used electronic health record data to identify patients (aged ≥20 years) who visited a VA ED from 2011 to 2019 with chest pain (CP), shortness of breath (SOB) or abdominal pain. They used practice pattern measures of the number of radiology and laboratory tests and hospital admission. Defined as primary outcomes were patient death within 30 days of ED visit and inpatient stays lasting less than 24 hours.

Taken into account were time (hour, day, month, year), location (ED, ED room), patient characteristics (age, sex, self-selected race and ethnicity [from VA-defined options], Elixhauser score, Emergency Severity Index [ESI]) and other physician characteristics (age, specialty).

Also, in a subanalysis of potentially low-value testing, the study team examined ordering of chest computed tomography (CT) scan with contrast as initial testing in patients with CP or SOB without high pretest probability for pulmonary embolism. In another subanalysis, they examined ordering of select laboratory tests (D-dimer and B-type natriuretic peptide [BNP] for CP and SOB; lipase for abdominal pain) and share of positive test results (test positivity). The authors noted that significant differences in test positivity would suggest differences in testing appropriateness.

Finally, to investigate types of patient factors associated with differences between female and male physicians, the study looked at Elixhauser score (<3, ≥3), ESI (≥3, <3), patient age (<65, ≥65 years) and patient sex. Analyses were conducted from Nov. 3, 2025, to June 3, 2026, using Stata 18.5 (StataCorp LLC).

The sample included about 1.6 million patient visits managed by 1,078 male and 448 female physicians across 105 VA EDs. The patients had a mean (SD) age of 62.59 (14.99) years and included about 1.4 million males (90.0%). The physicians had a mean (SD) age of 45.99 (10.49) years.

The results indicated that, within the same ED, differences in patient characteristics by physician sex were either not statistically or not clinically significant. “Female physicians ordered more tests and admitted a higher share of patients compared with male physicians (eg, share of patients with CP admitted: 45.7% vs 44.0%; 1.7 [95% CI, 1.2-2.2] percentage points higher),” the authors advised. “Across chief concerns, absolute differences ranged from 0.04 to 0.05 for number of radiology tests ordered, 0.21 to 0.33 for number of laboratory tests ordered, and 1.0 to 2.2 percentage points for share of patients admitted. There were no statistically significant differences by physician sex in mortality or likelihood of short inpatient stay.”

“In our first subanalysis, female vs. male physicians ordered more potentially low-value CT scans (eg, among patients with SOB, using our sensitive measure: 5.2% vs. 4.8%; 0.4 [95% CI, 0.2-0.6] percentage points higher),” the researchers explained. “In our second subanalysis, female vs. male physicians ordered more testing in 3 of 5 test for chief concern scenarios—D-dimer for CP and SOB and BNP for CP (eg, share of patients with SOB receiving D-dimer: 12.1% vs 11.0%; 1.1 [95% CI, 0.8-1.5] percentage points higher). No differences in test positivity were found across scenarios. In subgroup analyses, differences by physician sex were not consistently larger or smaller for patients with higher mortality risk (eg, higher Elixhauser score; more severe ESI).”

The authors concluded that female physicians ordered more tests and admitted more patients than male physicians in the same EDs, although differences were modest. “While this additional care was not associated with lower mortality, additional admitted patients were not more likely to be discharged within 24 hours, suggesting they had inpatient needs,” they advised. “Female physicians ordered more potentially low-value CT scans, but we could not assess differences in share of scans with a clinically significant finding. When we examined differences in test positivity, we found no differences, suggesting the additional tests ordered by female physicians may be clinically appropriate.”

Limitations of the study included specificity of findings to the VA setting, inability to determine whether more or fewer tests and admissions represent higher-quality care and use of older data.

The researchers suggested that their findings should remain relevant because sex-based differences, although small, likely will not dramatically change over time. “These modest differences may be associated with differences in risk aversion and peer judgment,” they suggested. “Female physicians may give greater consideration to other biopsychosocial factors, including symptom management, functional status and social support.”

title: Military Health System Sees Signs of Renewed Surgical Disparities Following COVID-19
description:
BETHESDA, MD — The Military Health System (MHS) is often cited as a model for reducing healthcare disparities because every beneficiary is covered by the same insurance.
Overall, the findings were favorable—readmissions rates did not differ significantly between military and civilian care settings, suggesting that the MHS continues to provide comparable surgical care regardless of where procedures are performed.
Previous reports indicated that surgical experience at military hospitals fell by approximately 36% during COVID-19, potentially affecting the experience of surgical teams and the efficiency of care delivery.

text:
BETHESDA, MD — The Military Health System (MHS) is often cited as a model for reducing healthcare disparities because every beneficiary is covered by the same insurance. For example, previous studies have indicated that, within the system, there has been no significant difference in rates of 90-day hospital readmissions after surgery—a measure of the effectiveness of the care provided—based upon race.

New research suggested, however, that disparities might be starting to reappear due to the MHS’s continued struggle with staff shortages, decreased number of surgeries being performed each year and long-term effects from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The new study, published in Annals of Surgery Open, was led by investigators at the Center for Health Services Research at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences in Bethesda together with researchers from the Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine and Harvard Medical School.

The authors suggested their study is the first to examine racial disparities in surgical outcomes within the different environments of care of the MHS following the COVID-19 pandemic.1

The researchers analyzed healthcare claims from more than 262,000 surgical procedures performed in 244,008 adult TRICARE beneficiaries between 2020 and 2023. They examined whether patients were readmitted to a hospital within 90 days of surgery, comparing outcomes at military treatment facilities (“direct care”) with those treated in civilian hospitals through the private sector.

Overall, the findings were favorable—readmissions rates did not differ significantly between military and civilian care settings, suggesting that the MHS continues to provide comparable surgical care regardless of where procedures are performed.

Closer examination showed some concerning disparities between particular groups of patients, however, according to the results. Black patients who had no major preexisting illnesses had a greater likelihood of being readmitted to the hospital within 90 days following their surgery, regardless of whether they were cared for at a military or civilian health facility. Hispanic patients with a single chronic illness also had a greater chance of readmission following surgery conducted at a military treatment center. On the other hand, Black and Hispanic patients with multiple chronic illnesses had fewer chances of being readmitted to the hospital following surgery conducted at a civilian health facility.

Although the differences were modest, the investigators said they worry that these might be warning signs. “We believe this reduction in care quality for racial and ethnic minorities is reflective of the workforce and staffing challenges, and reductions in meaningful procedural volume, that have confronted the Military Health System over the last decade and especially in the most recent three to five years that span the COVID-19 pandemic,” they wrote.

According to the authors, surgical volume within military treatment facilities has steadily declined over the past two decades, a trend that accelerated during the pandemic. Previous reports indicated that surgical experience at military hospitals fell by approximately 36% during COVID-19, potentially affecting the experience of surgical teams and the efficiency of care delivery.

The researchers say those systemwide pressures might disproportionately affect racial and ethnic minority patients. “Minority patients are likely the first to experience the effects of a struggling healthcare network due to previously recognized challenges in navigating healthcare utilization, reduced healthcare literacy, socioeconomic challenges that impact capacity to travel and greater risks of healthcare segregation,” they wrote.

The authors emphasized that the findings extend beyond military medicine. Because the MHS serves a large, geographically diverse population through a combination of military treatment facilities and civilian hospitals, they suggested that the results might provide important lessons for other large healthcare systems that rely on networks of tertiary referral centers and community hospitals.

“We believe the findings can serve as an informative model for other large healthcare networks that operate using a tiered system that combines large, tertiary referral centers with smaller community hospitals,” they wrote.

The study team said the findings carry two important messages: First, even healthcare systems with a strong history of reducing disparities can experience setbacks when staffing shortages, declining procedural volume or other operational pressures affect patient care. Second, looking only at overall quality measures might mask important differences affecting specific patient populations.

“Even if the overall performance of a system in terms of surgical care quality seems to be stable, certain segments of the population … may be experiencing healthcare disparities,” the authors wrote.

To address these concerns, the researchers recommended maintaining adequate staffing levels, increasing surgical volume within military treatment facilities when possible and routinely monitoring surgical outcomes by race, ethnicity and patient risk level.

“This message would seem to be as important for direct care facilities at this time as it is for civilian hospitals,” they concluded.

text:
Eligibility first

Start with DEERS and sponsor status

TRICARE coverage starts with the sponsor and beneficiary record. Confirm DEERS is current before choosing a plan, calling providers, or assuming a family member is covered.

Common groupsActive duty families, Guard and Reserve families, retirees, survivors, children, certain former spouses, Medicare-eligible beneficiaries, and other special categories may qualify.

Changing statusActivation, deactivation, retirement, Retired Reserve status, Medicare eligibility, relocation, marriage, birth, adoption, divorce, or sponsor death can change the TRICARE path.

Plan paths

Match the plan to the beneficiary

Prime, Select, US Family Health Plan, overseas options, Reserve Select, Retired Reserve, TRICARE Young Adult, and TRICARE For Life serve different groups and situations.

Active duty and familyActive duty service members generally follow Prime-style rules. Family members may have Prime, Select, overseas, US Family Health Plan, or Young Adult options depending on status and location.

Retired and Medicare eligibleRetired families may use Prime, Select, US Family Health Plan, Select Overseas, or TRICARE For Life. Medicare Part B is usually required when TRICARE and Medicare Part A eligibility overlap.

Provider verification

Verify network or authorized status before care

TRICARE directories and rules can differ by plan, region, provider type, and location. A provider lead is not the same as official network confirmation.

Ask billingConfirm whether the provider and exact location are network, non-network authorized, or unable to bill TRICARE for the plan and region.

Ask about costsBefore the appointment, ask about copay, cost-share, deductible, claim filing responsibility, and any balance-billing risk.

Referrals and authorization

Do not schedule specialty care blindly

Some TRICARE plans and services require a primary care manager referral, prior authorization, or approval tied to a specific provider, NPI, service, and location.

Get detailsAsk who requests the referral or authorization, what information is required, where it is sent, and whether you need a number before the visit.

Check service typeSpecialty care, therapy, mental health, maternity care, procedures, imaging, medications, and durable medical equipment may have different rules.

Regional contacts

Know who handles the region

TRICARE support depends on region and coverage type. If a provider cannot verify coverage, use the official contractor or TRICARE support path.

East and WestHumana Military handles East Region support. TriWest handles West Region support. Use the official TRICARE contact page when region or phone routing is unclear.

For Life and overseasWPS handles TRICARE For Life in the U.S. and territories. Overseas support is routed through official TRICARE Overseas resources.

VA Companion workflow

Use this site to prepare, then use TRICARE to finalize

VA Companion keeps planning tools, provider leads, scripts, and notes together. Official TRICARE systems remain the source for eligibility, enrollment, network status, referrals, authorizations, claim disputes, and billing corrections.

Prepare hereSearch provider leads, build the call script, identify plan and region, and write down what must be verified.

Finalize officiallyUse TRICARE, DEERS, milConnect, or the regional contractor before relying on coverage or scheduling rules.

Related guide

Looking for CHAMPVA instead?

CHAMPVA is separate from TRICARE and is generally for eligible spouses, survivors, dependent children, and some family caregivers tied to VA program rules. Use the CHAMPVA guide when the coverage is through VA instead of the military health system.

text:
The Government Accountability Office found that DOGE's claimed $110 billion in savings from contract, grant, and lease terminations were undermined by incorrect estimates, unverifiable calculations, and a lack of transparency about methodology.

According to the GAO report, auditors examined the savings figures DOGE posted to its "Wall of Receipts" website covering the period from January 20, 2025, through July 7, 2026. The watchdog found that DOGE did not use its stated methodology to calculate the majority of savings associated with terminated contracts, and could not verify the method used to calculate 96 percent of reported grant savings. DOGE officials did not respond to the GAO's requests for information or interviews.

Among the most notable findings: DOGE reported $1.7 billion in savings on a Department of Defense Defense Health Agency contract for IT services at more than 700 military treatment facilities worldwide. In the end, no action was taken to terminate the contract, reduce its scope, or deobligate any funds — meaning no savings were achieved.

On leases, the GAO determined that DOGE's claimed $113 million in savings across 264 lease terminations was inflated — the actual figure came to $53.5 million, leaving a $59.5 million gap between what was reported and what auditors could verify. Auditors also noted that 108 of those 264 leases had begun moving toward termination prior to DOGE's creation, with the savings attributable to those pre-existing actions totaling roughly $15.3 million.

For contracts, GAO auditors determined that 2,503 of the 13,476 contracts DOGE listed as terminated had not actually been cancelled at all, with those untouched contracts accounting for $27.4 billion in claimed savings. DOGE followed its stated savings methodology for contracts associated with only 27.5 percent of total reported contract savings.

The Wall of Receipts has not been updated since January 1, 2026, and a July 4, 2026, post on an official DOGE social media account indicated the organization's formal mission had ended. The site remained live as of July 7, 2026.

The GAO's sole recommendation called on the Executive Office of the President, acting through the U.S. DOGE Service, to make the Wall of Receipts' known data quality problems and methodological limitations clearly visible to anyone consulting the site. The U.S. DOGE Service did not provide comments on the report.

The report was requested by Democratic Sens. Gary Peters of Michigan and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, respectively.

"Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but DOGE was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement.

title: Does TRICARE Cover Ketamine Therapy? What to Know
description:
Ketamine infusions: possible, with steps For IV ketamine, TRICARE stands apart from most commercial insurers in that coverage is possible for qualifying diagnoses.
Our guides to what ketamine treatment costs and using FSA and HSA funds walk through the numbers.
Frequently asked questions Does TRICARE cover ketamine therapy?
TRICARE covers Spravato for treatment-resistant depression and major depression with suicidal thoughts, and may cover ketamine infusions for qualifying diagnoses with a referral and pre-authorization.
Does TRICARE cover ketamine or Spravato for PTSD?
text:
Short answer: TRICARE covers Spravato (esketamine) for adults with treatment-resistant depression or major depression with suicidal thoughts, and, unusually among insurers, it may also cover ketamine infusions for qualifying diagnoses, though a referral and pre-authorization are typically required and approval is case by case. PTSD alone generally does not qualify. Here is how to navigate it.

The short version of a complicated answer

Military families ask us this often, and the answer is more hopeful than for most insurance. Where the majority of commercial insurers decline IV ketamine entirely because it is off-label, TRICARE evaluates it case by case for qualifying mental health and pain diagnoses. Coverage is not guaranteed, the paperwork is real, and the details depend on your plan and diagnosis, but the door is genuinely open in a way it is not with many insurers.

What TRICARE covers most clearly: Spravato

The most established coverage path is Spravato, the FDA-approved esketamine nasal spray. TRICARE covers it for adults 18 and older with treatment-resistant depression, generally meaning at least two adequate antidepressant trials without sufficient response, or major depressive disorder with suicidal thoughts or behavior. Because Spravato is on-label and FDA approved for these diagnoses, the approval pathway is more standardized. Note that PTSD alone is not a covered diagnosis for Spravato.

Ketamine infusions: possible, with steps

For IV ketamine, TRICARE stands apart from most commercial insurers in that coverage is possible for qualifying diagnoses. Expect to need a referral from your provider, pre-authorization before treatment begins, and documentation of your diagnosis and treatment history. Each case is evaluated individually, so two people with similar stories can get different answers. The practical move is to call the number on your TRICARE card, ask specifically about ketamine infusion coverage for your diagnosis and plan, and get any approval in writing before scheduling.

Veterans and the VA

If your care runs through the VA rather than TRICARE, ketamine and Spravato may be accessible through VA facilities or the VA community care program, which has its own clinical criteria and referral process. It is a separate system with separate rules, so ask your VA mental health provider about eligibility.

If coverage falls short

If TRICARE declines or the process stalls, treatment can still be within reach. FSA and HSA funds can generally be used for ketamine therapy, and we offer in-house financing that spreads the cost into manageable monthly payments. Our guides to what ketamine treatment costs and using FSA and HSA funds walk through the numbers. And given how common PTSD and depression are among those who serve, we wrote separately about ketamine therapy for first responders and PTSD.

This article is for educational purposes only and is not medical, legal, or insurance advice. Verify your specific coverage with TRICARE directly, as policies and determinations vary.

The bottom line

TRICARE covers Spravato for qualifying depression diagnoses and may cover ketamine infusions with a referral and pre-authorization, which makes it one of the more workable insurers for this treatment. Get the specifics for your plan in writing, and if coverage falls short, financing and FSA or HSA funds can bridge the gap. If you are a military family exploring options, call us at (310) 280-4440 and we will help you think it through.

Frequently asked questions

Does TRICARE cover ketamine therapy? TRICARE covers Spravato for treatment-resistant depression and major depression with suicidal thoughts, and may cover ketamine infusions for qualifying diagnoses with a referral and pre-authorization. Approval is case by case.

Does TRICARE cover ketamine or Spravato for PTSD? PTSD alone is generally not a covered diagnosis for Spravato. If depression is also present, coverage may be possible under the depression diagnosis. Verify with TRICARE for your situation.

What do I need for TRICARE to consider covering ketamine infusions? Typically a referral from your provider, pre-authorization before treatment, and documentation of your diagnosis and prior treatment history. Get approvals in writing.

title: Get to know how TRICARE covers your college student - Joint Base San Antonio
description:
“Different TRICARE plans have different rules for getting care, so it’s important to know how your child’s current plan will work in the new location,” said Debra Fisher, TRICARE health system specialist, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency.
Which TRICARE plan will work best for your child Your child’s TRICARE plan and school’s location may affect how he or she gets care when away at college.
Moving to a new location may also affect your child’s TRICARE plan options.
There are a few ways to change your child’s TRICARE plan: Change his or her address in DEERS to their college address.
The college will have a deadline for submitting proof of TRICARE coverage or other health coverage each year.
text:
Going to college is an exciting milestone for many young adults. From signing up for classes to buying dorm supplies, summer can be a busy time for new college students and their families. During this time, you’ll also need to make sure your child’s TRICARE coverage will be ready when the semester starts, especially if he or she is moving away from home.

“Different TRICARE plans have different rules for getting care, so it’s important to know how your child’s current plan will work in the new location,” said Debra Fisher, TRICARE health system specialist, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency. “You may be able to change your child’s plan when he or she moves away for college.”

As you help your child prepare for the start of college, keep these things in mind.

1. Which TRICARE plan will work best for your child

Your child’s TRICARE plan and school’s location may affect how he or she gets care when away at college. Moving to a new location may also affect your child’s TRICARE plan options. These things are especially true if your child has a TRICARE Prime plan.

With TRICARE Prime, you may pay point-of-service fees if your child gets nonemergency care without a referral from their primary care manager. This may include care your child gets at the college’s student health center.

If your child moves far away from home, you may want to consider TRICARE Select. Your child can visit any TRICARE-authorized provider while at school without a referral. He or she will also have more flexibility for getting care when home during school breaks.

There are a few ways to change your child’s TRICARE plan:

Change his or her address in DEERS to their college address. This will trigger a TRICARE Qualifying Life Event. A QLE opens a 90-day window for your child to change plans. (Other members of your family may be able to change plans during this window too.)

Make changes during TRICARE Open Season. The next TRICARE Open Season is Nov. 9–Dec. 8, 2026. Keep in mind that changes you make during open season won’t take effect until Jan. 1, 2027.

You can check the Plan Finder to see which TRICARE plans may be available to your child.

Is your child enrolled in TRICARE Reserve Select or TRICARE Retired Reserve? You don’t need to make changes to their plan. With these plans, your child can visit any TRICARE-authorized provider without a referral.

2. The college’s requirements

Most U.S. colleges require full-time students to have health insurance. In general, TRICARE health plans meet this requirement. However, be sure to check with your child’s college to confirm its requirements.

The college will have a deadline for submitting proof of TRICARE coverage or other health coverage each year. If you don’t do this by the deadline, your student may be required to buy the school’s health insurance plan. If your child is enrolled in the school’s health insurance plan, this is considered other health insurance. You must report OHI to TRICARE.

The college may also require your child to get a physical exam. TRICARE covers physicals when they’re required for school enrollment. (Keep in mind that TRICARE doesn’t cover sports physicals.)

3. Staying eligible for TRICARE

Being enrolled in college full-time may allow your child to stay enrolled in a TRICARE health plan until he or she graduates or turns age 23 — whichever comes first. (Otherwise, eligibility for “regular” TRICARE coverage will end at age 21.)

Before your child turns 21, you’ll need to go to your local Uniformed Services ID card office to show that your child:

Is a full-time student at an approved institution of higher learning in pursuit of an associate’s degree or higher—you’ll need a letter from the school’s registrar office to demonstrate this.

Isn’t married

Depends on you (their sponsor) for more than 50% of his or her financial support

Go to milConnect to learn more about these requirements and staying eligible for TRICARE as a full-time student.

After your child’s eligibility for “regular” TRICARE coverage ends, your child may be able to buy TRICARE Young Adult coverage until age 26. Eligibility for TYA is based on several factors, as outlined in the TRICARE Young Adult Fact Sheet. These factors include your child’s marital status and eligibility for employer-sponsored health insurance. Children who are eligible can buy TYA at any time. TRICARE Open Season and TRICARE Qualifying Life Events don’t apply to TYA.

After losing eligibility for TRICARE or TYA, your child may be eligible to buy Continued Health Care Benefit Program coverage.

TYA and CHCBP might not be your child’s only health coverage options when losing eligibility for TRICARE. For example, your child may be able to buy a health plan through the Health Insurance Marketplace.

By knowing how your child’s health coverage options may change during college and after graduation, you can help your child have the health coverage that meets his or her needs.

text:
OIG Finds Veterans Aren’t Being Properly Informed of Options

WASHINGTON, DC — The VA recently announced that it had made more than $36 billion in payments to local healthcare providers across the country in fiscal year 2025 as part of the VA MISSION Act.

That was another substantial jump in spending on community care, which has more than quintupled since 2014, when $8 billion was spent; the VA paid out $31 billion in 2024. That has created concerns that the Trump administration is increasing its efforts to “privatize” care for veterans.

One of the strongest critics has been Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-IL, an Iraq War veteran who lost both legs in combat. “I see clear as day that the end goal here is to privatize and eventually dismantle the VA,” she said earlier this year, accusing the administration of cutting the VA workforce, undermining labor protections and moving care away from VA clinicians.

President Donald Trump signed the MISSION Act in 2018 after it passed Congress with bipartisan support. The law expanded a benefit to allow eligible veterans to choose care from authorized local, non-VA healthcare providers at VA expense. The Veterans Community Care Program, which is the fourth largest healthcare payer program in America, pays for the care.

Last year, the bipartisan Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act required VA to ensure that veterans and their referring clinicians can choose community care without any additional review when it’s in the patient’s best medical interest. Under current law, veterans also can choose community care in other circumstances, including if their average driving time or wait time exceeds certain thresholds or when they need a service that is not provided by a VA facility.

In a press release last month, the VA touted a March 2026 survey from Rasmussen Reports finding that 90% of likely military voters support the policy.

In fiscal year 2025, it said, the top 10 states where providers received the most funding from VA community care were:

Texas, $3.3 billion

Florida, $2.8 billion

California, $2.1 billion

North Carolina, $1.5 billion

Ohio, $1.3 billion

Tennessee, $1.2 billion

Pennsylvania, $1.1 billion

Michigan, $1.0 billion

Georgia, $1.0 billion

Arizona, $1.0 billion

“VA community care is a vital benefit that ensures the health of both Veterans and the local economies where they live,” VA Secretary Doug Collins said in the press release.

The process has not gone as smoothly as the VA has often suggested, however, A recent audit by the VA’s Office of Inspector General (OIG) estimated that VHA could have potentially avoided spending $440 million (or $1.7 billion in monetary benefits over a full fiscal year) on community care if schedulers had consistently made accurate eligibility determinations and referred veterans to VAMCs with available services.

Acknowledging that, at the time of publication of this report, the VHA “had planned significant changes to the structure of its management and operations. The findings and recommendations in this report can help guide VHA’s reorganization efforts and implementation.”

The audit team reviewed VA appointment and community care consult data from Oct. 1 through Dec. 31, 2024—the first quarter of fiscal year (FY) 2025—and the final claims data for these consults as of July 2025. The team’s fieldwork continued through February 2026, which collectively served as the basis for the findings and recommendations in this report.

“The OIG found that VHA is not effectively identifying and informing all eligible veterans about all their care options within and outside VA,” according to an executive summary. “Not only were some eligible veterans not informed of their entitlement to community care, but ineligible veterans were also improperly approved for it—risking both underutilization and misuse of the Veterans Community Care Program.”

The VA OIG pointed out that, during briefings in September and October 2025, VHA leaders confirmed that the challenges identified in this report were still present and that they had not yet implemented solutions to the scheduling issues identified.

For example, Larry M. Reinkemeyer, assistant inspector general for audits and evaluations, wrote, “VHA schedulers cannot always schedule at other VA medical facilities that could have provided care within the wait-time and drive-time standards because of scheduling system limitations. Furthermore, VHA lacks the ability to assess the accuracy of wait-time eligibility determinations.”

Specifically, OIG testing revealed that medical facility staff referred about 25% of community-care consults for mental healthcare or specialty care—an estimated 340,000 of 1.4 million total consults—to providers outside VA, even though veterans did not meet eligibility requirements. Staff also referred an estimated 38% of appointments—about 1.8 million of about 4.8 million—to VA facilities, even though they were eligible for community care; no assessment of these veterans’ eligibility for community care was documented.

“These issues arose because guidance from VA’s Office of Integrated Veteran Care (IVC) was inconsistent with the MISSION Act and due to scheduling system limitations, which prevented schedulers from seeing appointment availability across all VA medical facilities that were within wait-time and drive-time standards,” the OIG advised.

The report also pointed out that veterans weren’t informed about which care option was most expedient, because schedulers lacked full access to community care wait-time data. In about 13% of wait time-eligible community care consults (about 38,100 of 287,000), the veteran could have received care faster by opting out of community care and taking the next available VA appointment, according to the government watchdog group, which added, “Conversely, about 58 percent of primary care, mental health care, or specialty care appointments occurring within VA that the OIG identified as eligible for community care (about 1.1 million of about 1.8 million) had no documentation that the veteran had opted out of community care—meaning there was no evidence these veterans knew all their care options before they were scheduled for direct care within VA.”

The OIG suggested that recent changes, such as the expansion of VHA’s External Provider Scheduling System, which allows VA to schedule directly into participating community provider schedules, “show progress toward addressing these issues.”

“This audit is critical for several reasons,” the report stated. “First, accurately identifying and informing eligible veterans of their right to receive community care is essential to ensuring timely access to treatment. When veterans are not made aware of their eligibility, they may face avoidable delays. At the same time, approving veterans who do not meet program requirements can result in unnecessary expenditures and place additional strain on a costly program.”

In a press release, the VA noted, “While community care is an important option for many veterans, VA is also spending record amounts of funding on direct care—a record high $101 billion was spent on direct care in FY 2025, when VA completed a record high 82,083,918 direct care appointments, up 4.1% from FY 2024.”

At the same time, the increase in expenditures for community care exceeded 18%.

text:
DHA said its test environment has grown past what programs actually use, with deferred hardware refreshes leaving aging infrastructure

Phase 1 submissions are due Aug. 20

Awards will be fixed-price only, tied to delivered results rather than labor hours

The Defense Health Agency has told industry that the test infrastructure behind its health IT programs costs more than it returns, and is asking companies to propose commercial fixes. DHA’s contracting activity posted a commercial solutions opening Wednesday on SAM.gov for Enterprise Support Services Next, on behalf of Program Executive Office Defense Healthcare Management Systems.

Phase 1 submissions will close Aug. 20. Any resulting contracts will be fixed-price and tied to tangible results, with the agency stating it cannot award on a level-of-effort or labor-hour basis.

Technology, AI and modernization priorities at DHA, HHS and the Veterans Health Administration are on the agenda at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3. Register now!

What Problem Is DHA Trying to Solve?

Individual programs were handed infrastructure and left to configure and manage it themselves, an arrangement the agency says offered early flexibility but produced uncoordinated growth that far exceeds operational demand. Hardware refresh cycles were deferred, leaving equipment that costs more to maintain.

Three consequences follow: the agency pays for capacity nobody uses, program staff who should be building products spend their time administering infrastructure instead, and DHA lacks the utilization and cost visibility to confirm its spending matches mission need.

The agency called these problems structural and said that better management of the existing contract would not resolve them. No single entity is accountable for the environment’s performance or cost, it said.

What Is DHA Asking Industry to Deliver?

Five goals were listed in the announcement, three of them immediate.

The first covers the consolidation of infrastructure and facilities, with different constraints by program. Joint Operational Medicine Information Systems work must retain hardware-in-the-loop capability for simulating disconnected, intermittent and low-bandwidth tactical conditions, including physical device handshakes. Defense Healthcare Management Systems testing of medical devices and peripherals, by contrast, should explore moving out of centralized lab space, whether into virtualized environments, military treatment facilities or something else that measurably shrinks the footprint.

The second turns the service model from a workspace that tenants configure into a governed platform, with automated provisioning, self-service capabilities with security guardrails and continuous license rationalization. DHA specified that total cost of ownership calculations must account for its own lifecycle cost estimate components and its Amazon Web Services spending, not just the contractor’s price.

The third places cybersecurity accountability on the contractor, covering continuous authorization, vulnerability remediation and progress toward zero trust maturity.

Two further goals are structured as options that DHA will exercise later, with timing depending on when other contracts end. One covers developmental test and evaluation and independent verification and validation work. The other consolidates enterprise tooling onto Software Development Lifecycle Next as the standard platform.

How Will DHA Evaluate Submissions?

Phase 1 asks for a paper of no more than five pages, or 15 briefing slides, describing the concept and a rough order-of-magnitude cost. Selected companies move to Phase 2, where DHA requests a contractor-drafted performance work statement and pricing, plus at least one collaborative session the agency describes as mutual due diligence.

DHA named Boston Consulting Group and Andrew Morgan as non-government advisers who will review submissions.

title: GAO says DOGE couldn't substantiate much of its claimed savings - The Black Chronicle
description:
