text:
President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency claimed it saved taxpayers $1.7 billion by identifying a single Pentagon health contract, but the contract was never canceled and taxpayers didn’t save any money, a federal watchdog found.

The Government Accountability Office released its report Thursday. It found that DOGE did not follow its own stated method for calculating most of the savings it reported from terminated contracts. For grants, DOGE did not provide enough information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of its reported savings. And it found DOGE overstated lease savings by more than $80 million.

DOGE’s temporary organization formally shut down July 4 under the executive order that created it. The broader U.S. DOGE Service continues. As of July 7, the Wall of Receipts remained live and had not been updated since Jan. 1. The disputed savings figures were still posted as of Thursday.

In one case, GAO found, DOGE claimed more than $1.7 billion in savings on a Defense Health Agency contract for IT support at more than 700 military medical facilities worldwide. DOGE initially flagged the contract for termination. But after meeting with Pentagon officials, it agreed no action should be taken. The contract was not canceled, so no money was saved, GAO found. The claimed $1.7 billion in savings still appears on the live Wall of Receipts page.

The $110 billion GAO reviewed covers only DOGE’s claimed savings from contracts, grants and leases. DOGE’s website reports $215 billion in total savings across all categories, including asset sales, workforce reductions and regulatory changes. That figure has not changed since Jan. 1. It is a fraction of the $2 trillion Elon Musk initially suggested.

The report was requested by Sens. Gary Peters, D-Mich., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrats on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Peters called DOGE “a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people.” He said it “claimed billions of dollars in savings it could not substantiate” and “took credit for work already underway.”

Blumenthal said the findings make DOGE’s savings “unreliable and unclear.”

In response to questions about the report’s findings, a White House official addressed only DOGE employees’ ethics training and financial disclosure requirements, not the savings claims. The U.S. DOGE Service did not provide comments to GAO.

The report lands as the Trump administration has shifted its anti-fraud strategy. On the same day GAO published its findings, the White House launched Fraud.gov, another government site posting a large top-line savings figure, nearly $230 billion, for public view.

text:
The US efficiency agency lied about terminating leases and published unverified grant cuts, the Government Accountability Office has found

The US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), suggested and initially spearheaded by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, credited itself with billions of dollars in federal budget savings that could not be independently verified, a government watchdog said Thursday.

US President Donald Trump launched the now-defunct initiative shortly after he took office last January, tapping Musk as his government efficiency czar. The agency was billed as a sweeping effort to cut waste and bureaucracy across the federal government and its sprawling $7 trillion annual budget.

DOGE claims to have saved around $215 billion - just over 3% of the federal budget - through contract and lease cancellations, grant cuts, workforce reductions, regulatory changes and other actions.

However, billions of the roughly $110 billion in savings published on DOGE's 'Wall of Receipts' were either "incorrect or lacked supporting evidence," the US Government Accountability Office found.

DOGE provided insufficient information to verify 96% of the $49.2 billion it claimed to have saved from terminating nearly 16,000 grants, the watchdog reported.

Auditors also found that more than a third of the lease terminations credited to DOGE, worth around $15.3 million, were already being phased out before the initiative was established.

In one case, DOGE claimed $1.7 billion in savings from a Defense Health Agency IT contract covering more than 700 military treatment facilities. The contract, however, was never terminated or reduced, GAO wrote. "Thus, no savings were achieved," it said.

DOGE officially shut down in July, following months of rumors that the initiative was quietly being dismantled and its functions absorbed elsewhere in the federal government.

Its final tally fell far short of Musk's early promises. Before the start of Trump's second term, the tech mogul claimed that DOGE could slash as much as $2 trillion from federal spending, later scaling back that target.

The aggressive campaign quickly became a political flashpoint as tens of thousands of federal workers lost their jobs and government programs were targeted for cuts. Musk also clashed with several senior officials in Trump's cabinet before publicly feuding with the president over the Big Beautiful Bill, calling it a "disgusting abomination" and accusing it of exacerbating the ballooning US budget deficit.

text:
DEERS is the record everything else depends on

The Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System holds who you are, who your family members are, and where you live. Coverage decisions, claim payments, and every piece of mail TRICARE sends you follow the address in DEERS, so a stale address there produces problems that look like plan problems.

TRICARE publishes four ways to update your contact information: online through ID Card Online at idco.dmdc.osd.mil, by phone on the DEERS Support Office line published on that page, by fax to (800) 336-4416 or (502) 335-9980, and by mail to the DMDC/DEERS Support Office in Seaside, California. Family members can update contact information once they are registered.

One constraint from TRICARE's own instruction: the address you supply has to be a physical address. A P.O. box will not be accepted.

Enrollment and claims route to your regional contractor

TRICARE is administered by regional contractors, and the destination for an enrollment form or a claim is set by the region, not by TRICARE centrally. There is no national TRICARE enrollment fax and no national claims fax to publish, so this page does not invent one.

Where to find yours:

The enrollment form itself. The regional version of the form carries its own submission instructions.

Your regional contractor's contact page, reached from the regions section of tricare.mil.

The letter you received. A request for documents names the destination for those documents.

The back of your uniformed services ID card, for the phone number that can tell you the rest.

If you are sending a claim, check whether the claims processor for your region takes them by mail only. Several do.

How to fax TRICARE paperwork without a fax machine

Create a free FaxTerra account with an email address, upload the completed form as a PDF or as photos taken with your phone, enter the fax number for the office you are writing to, and send. A delivery confirmation arrives by email, which is worth keeping for anything with a deadline attached.

Small documents send free within your monthly free pages, and longer packets are covered by a one-time credit pack from about 10¢ a page. text:
AUGUSTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - Georgia Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock are renewing their push to save inpatient care at Fort Gordon’s Eisenhower Army Medical Center.

Saying troops, families and veterans in the Augusta area deserve clearer answers, Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock this week sent a new letter to War Department officials after the agency missed a response deadline the senators set in June.

The lawmakers are urging the Defense Health Agency to abandon a plan to convert the hospital into an ambulatory care center.

Inpatient care at Eisenhower would be permanently shut down and the emergency room would be downgraded to an urgent care center.

Ossoff and Warnock say those changes could disrupt medical care for servicemembers, their families and veterans.

They also say it would add strain to Augusta’s civilian health care system.

The senators also argue the Pentagon has not fully explained what services would be affected or how the transition would work.

“Seventeen days have passed since the deadline stated in our letter seeking more information about DHA’s decision to close all inpatient services at Dwight D. Eisenhower Army Medical Center (DDEAMC) and transition the facility to an ambulatory care center, and we have not received a response,” Ossoff and Warnock wrote to Department of Defense Assistant Secretary Keith Bass and DHA Director Vice Adm. Darin Via, calling the lack of reply “unacceptable.”

“Servicemembers, their families, and veterans in Augusta deserve answers and information on how these potential changes could affect their ability to receive quality health care,” they added.

In their latest inquiry, the senators are asking DHA to immediately withdraw its formal notification to Congress about modifying services at Eisenhower until more details are provided and the potential impact is better understood.

Ossoff first questioned the proposed reductions in a separate letter to the agency last November.

The renewed push in the Senate follows action in the U.S. House earlier this year. As previously reported, Rep. Rick Allen, R‑Augusta, backed provisions in the House-passed National Defense Authorization Act that would block or roll back changes to the “scope of medical services” at certain military medical facilities, a move his office said was aimed in part at protecting Eisenhower.

text:
When Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency launched its effort to slash federal spending last year, it also created a website to show how much money it said it was saving taxpayers.

A new review by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found the site's claim of $110 billion in taxpayer savings was vastly inflated and unreliable.

The report found DOGE could not provide enough information to verify 96% of its reported savings from canceled grants.

Despite its pledge of transparency, the report found DOGE did not use its stated methodology to calculate about half of the savings it reported.

“Because U.S. DOGE Service officials did not respond to requests for information, GAO could not determine the reasons why DOGE did not disclose data quality issues and limitations when the website first went live or at any time since then,” the report said.

The report also found DOGE failed to terminate some of the contracts it claimed to have canceled. According to the report, $27.4 billion in claimed savings was never executed, and DOGE did not provide identifying information for another $7.2 billion in claimed savings.

DOGE also claimed $1.7 billion in savings from an IT services contract for the Defense Department's Defense Health Agency, but the report said no changes were ever made.

The report also said DOGE claimed savings from millions of dollars in leases that had already been identified for termination.

Musk has since left DOGE. ABC News reached out to Musk and the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Although DOGE formally ended on July 4, its "Wall of Receipts" remains online, claiming a total of $215 billion in taxpayer savings.

text:
Men aged 65 years or older are significantly more likely than younger men to experience postsurgical complications following radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer, according to research published in Clinical Genitourinary Cancer.

“In the US Military Health System, which provides access to comprehensive medical

care for patients of all ages, we found age differences in short- and long-term complication rates following [radical prostatectomy] among men with prostate cancer,” study investigators wrote. “Age ≥65 years was associated with a higher risk of general and [genitourinary] complications and readmissions in the 90-day postoperative period relative to age 55-64 years. … Meanwhile, age <55 years was not associated with statistical differences in complications compared to age 55-64.”

The investigators identified 5139 adult men who were diagnosed with prostate adenocarcinoma between 2001 and 2014 and underwent radical prostatectomy within 1 year of diagnosis. All patients were treated in the Military Health System, which provides universal health care to active or retired service members and eligible dependents.

The patients were categorized as young (aged 18-54 years; n=1627), middle-aged (aged 55-64 years; n=2543), and older (aged 65 years or older; n=969).

Young and middle-aged men were more likely to be treated at a private civilian facility compared to older men, the researchers reported. Older men were more likely to undergo open procedures and less likely to receive laparoscopic or robotic-assisted procedures compared to the other age groups. Older men were also more likely to have pelvic lymph node dissection and to have a higher number of lymph nodes examined.

Older men received adjuvant hormone treatment (7.6%) more often than men in the other age groups. The investigators observed no differences in the frequency of adjuvant radiation or chemotherapy across age groups.

Overall, 5.1% of study patients experienced a general complication at 90 days after surgery. About 28% had a genitourinary complication, and 4.2% were readmitted.

Patients in the oldest cohort had the highest frequency of general complications (8.6%) and readmission (5.9%) compared with the other age groups (Chi-square P <.05). Age had no apparent effect on the frequency of genitourinary complications (Chi-square P =.28).

In regression analysis, younger men had a 25% lower risk of general complications at 90 days post-surgery compared to the other age groups. However, that result was not statistically significant in adjusted models (adjusted risk ratios [ARR], 0.75; 95% CI, 0.54-1.03).

Older men had a 72% greater risk for general complications (ARR, 1.72; 95% CI, 1.31-2.27) compared with the middle-aged cohort after the researchers adjusted for patient, tumor, and surgery characteristics.

“This result confirms findings from the earlier studies and highlights the need for continued monitoring of older patients after [radical prostatectomy] and implementation of risk-management strategies and early interventions if complications occur to further prevent readmission,” the investigators wrote.

Overall, age older than 65 years was associated with higher risk for genitourinary complications (ARR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.01-1.27) and readmissions (ARR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.05-1.99) compared with age 55-64 years.

The overall 18-month genitourinary complication rates were 19.8% for patients who did not receive adjuvant radiation therapy and 20.9% among those who did.

Among those who did not receive adjuvant radiation, men in the oldest cohort were at greater risk for urinary incontinence (ARR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.15-2.08) and bladder neck contracture (ARR, 1.88, 95% CI, 1.08-3.27) compared with middle-aged men.

text:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted premarket clearance to a 3D printed titanium cranial plate developed at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, marking the first time the agency has cleared an implant produced by a point-of-care institution.

The clearance, listed under submission number K253116, covers the 3D Medical Applications Center’s (3D MAC) Titanium Cranial Plate (TCP) System, developed with support from the Defense Health Agency (DHA) and 3D Systems.

The device is designed to reconstruct complex cranial and facial defects caused by trauma, disease, or cancer, and will be used to treat active-duty personnel and war fighters suffering traumatic head injuries around the world.

A design built for the operating room

Dr. Peter Liacouras, director of services at 3D MAC, designed the plate so that hardware doesn’t need to be added separately during surgery. “One feature of the TCP is that the fixation bars are already incorporated into the design, so you can simply place it and screw it down,” Liacouras said. For surgical teams treating combat injuries, that shortens a step in an already time-sensitive procedure.

3D MAC has built anatomical models, surgical guides, and implants for years, but those tools generally support surgical planning rather than becoming part of the patient, so they don’t require individual FDA sign-off the way an implant does. The TCP System is the center’s first product to undergo the full 510(k) process itself, with the center handling its production instead of relying on a physician-directed custom-device pathway or an outside manufacturer.

Building the regulatory track record

Reaching that bar took a multi-year effort. 3D Systems said it helped 3D MAC establish a quality management system and supported the project through design optimization, manufacturing process validation, and the submission itself.

“This clearance underscores the power of combining clinical innovation with deep expertise in additive manufacturing and regulatory compliance,” said Natalie Byrnes, 3D Systems’ manager of product development for patient-specific medical technology. “We are honored to help enable expanded access to personalized care delivered at the point of treatment.”

CEO Jeff Graves called the milestone validation of the company’s broader strategy: “We believe point-of-care manufacturing is transforming the future of healthcare by bringing personalized medical devices closer to the patient. Our unique collaborations with the U.S. Defense Health Agency and the Department of Veterans Affairs underscore our leadership in this space and reinforce our commitment to expanding this business as a long-term growth driver for 3D Systems.”

What it opens up for military hospitals

Because 3D MAC holds the 510(k) clearance itself, its design and manufacturing process can be used at other approved military treatment facilities beyond Walter Reed.

U.S. Army Lt. Col. Andrea Mountney, deputy director of the DHA’s Office of Regulatory Activities, said the approval speeds up how quickly wounded troops get custom hardware: “By securing 510(k) clearance for the 3D MAC Titanium Cranial Plate System, we are delivering personalized patient-unique implants at the point-of-care – accelerating casualty treatment, sharpening surgical outcomes and speeding the recovery of our wounded service members,” she said, adding that additive manufacturing “puts a critical capability directly into the hands of our military providers.”

From supplier-led to institution-led clearance

The Walter Reed result marks a shift in how 3D Systems has pursued point-of-care manufacturing. In earlier programs, the FDA or MDR clearance sat with a system 3D Systems had already cleared, and the hospital operated within it. Here, 3D MAC itself holds the clearance as the regulated manufacturer of record, a distinction that lets it expand the device to other sites.

That earlier model is visible in 3D Systems’ work with University Hospital Basel, where the company’s VSP PEEK Cranial Implant solution became the first cranial implant produced at the point of care under current MDR rules, followed in 2025 by what 3D Systems called the world’s first point-of-care facial implant. In both cases, the clearance belonged to 3D Systems’ own workflow, not the treating hospital.

Other companies are approaching the same territory from different angles. Ricoh USA’s 3D for Healthcare Innovation Studio lets clinicians design and print FDA-cleared anatomic models on-site, and 3D LifePrints (now Insight Surgery) markets its EmbedMed platform directly to hospitals looking to stand up their own point-of-care 3D printing operations. None of these programs has yet put an implant through clearance under the treating institution’s own name.

That’s what makes the Walter Reed clearance significant. It shows a hospital lab can own FDA clearance outright, instead of borrowing it through a vendor’s system.
